game:item-handbooktext-boat-sailed-*:
Sailboats are constructed in place on land, and then rolled into the water. They cannot be picked up. They can be deconstructed by holding down rightmouse with a saw. See the Building A Sailboat entry for more information.

Movement
Once you have constructed your sailboat, rightmouse click on the starboard aft seat (by the tiller at the stern) to sit in that seat: only that seat can control the boat. With the sails furled, you can use normal navigation keys to move the boat slowly. rightmouse-click on the cleat on the side of the mast (where a rope is tied) to unfurl the sail and pick up speed. The sailboat currently does not respond to wind direction, only your movement keys.

If the boat becomes grounded or in water that is too shallow, it can be moved very slowly using the arrow keys, but only with the sail furled again.

Equipping
Most boat accessories are added to the boat via ctrl + rightmouse.
The boat can also hold several passengers - in every boat, one passenger can sit on the port-side aft seat (adjacent to the player who is at the tiller controlling the boat). Additional seats can be added to any of the eight cargo hold spots.

You can place containers (including chests, baskets, and storage vessels) in the hold of the boat, and access them on or off the boat.

You can also place a mount (such as an elk) on the boat by first placing a wooden fence post in one of the cargo spots - being sure to leave 2 cargo spots empty aft of the post - and then using a rope on this fence post, which will place the animal into the aft cargo spots. You can then disembark the animal using rightmouse on the fence post.

You can attach a lantern to the aft face of the mast (about 3 meters up) to provide light.

Ratlines can be attached to the gunwhales on each side of the mast in order to allow you to climb to the top of the mast to look around.

An anchor can be placed in the front-left space in the prow. With an empty hand, rightmouse click it to let it go or haul it up; see Mooring and Anchoring.

There is also a spot at the prow for a figurehead to be placed (you can also place your own chiseled figurehead there), and on the port bow, your boat can be named (using pigment and shift + rightmouse-click).
game:item-handbooktext-anchor-stone: The stone anchor can be placed in the front-left prow location of the sailboat (and only this spot). With an empty hand, rightmouse click it to let it go or haul it up. It holds when about five times the depth of the water in rope is let out; see Mooring and Anchoring.

itemdesc-bark-*: Peeled from a log with a knife. It builds a bark canoe, and mends one on the way.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:re:
Quick to bind from reeds with a knife and light to carry. Blows and breakers spring off its bundles, though a hard knock on rock tears them, and it soaks up water: after about three days afloat it lies on the bottom. Dry it ashore in the sun between trips; each drying leaves it a little more rotten, and it cannot be mended. It carries one person and a basket.
- Place it with a rightmouse click and paddle it with the paddle it carries: no oar is needed.
- Pick it up with shift + rightmouse.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:du:
One log hollowed out: the toughest hull before planks, barely scratched by rocks, and it needs no upkeep. Too heavy to carry; a workhorse of rivers and lakes. Tippy in a sea: it rolls hard and ships water over its low sides; bail it with a bowl, jug or bucket before it swamps.

Building it
A dugout is burnt and hewn out of one trunk, beside the water it will float on.
- Lay five logs of one wood on their sides, end to end along the shore, with water in the very next blocks.
- Light a fire on the middle log with a torch or a firestarter. The logs become a blank, and the fire chars its top for about a day.
- Hew out the char with an axe: rightmouse.
- Then, a day at a time: smear wet clay along the rim with rightmouse, so that the fire eats only the hollow, light the fire again, and hew out the char once it burns out. Six burns hollow her out. Rain puts the fire out; light it again.
- Push her into the water with shift + rightmouse and an empty hand: a heavy blank takes many pushes. She floats, and an axe breaks her up, at every stage, but she gets her seats only when finished.

Using it
- Paddle it from the front seat with an oar in hand. The back seat carries a passenger.
- Mend it with a log of its wood.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:co:
A round bowl of hide for one. It spins on the spot and is poor in a straight line: for fishing and short crossings. It is light enough to wear on your back.
- Scull it over the bow with the paddle it carries: no oar is needed.
- Pick it up with shift + rightmouse, and put it in a backpack slot to carry it on your back.
- Mend it with a small prepared hide.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:ba:
Bark on a light frame: fast, with a draft so shallow that it runs rapids which batter every other hull. Fragile, and carried over portages.
- Paddle it from the back seat with the paddle it carries: no oar is needed. The front seat carries a passenger.
- Pick it up with shift + rightmouse.
- Mend it on the way with bark of the same tree.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:cu:
Greased hide on a wooden frame: light, and it carries cargo along the coast under oars. Rocks hole the hide, and its seams seep unless greased with rendered fat every few days afloat. The light hull flexes with the sea and rides over swells that come aboard heavier boats.
- Row it from the stern thwart with its own pair of oars: no oar is needed.
- Its bottom carries three baskets, storage vessels or chests, forward of the rower: ctrl + rightmouse puts one in its place.
- Pick it up with shift + rightmouse.
- Grease it with rendered fat to stop the seams seeping, and mend holes in the hide with a large prepared hide.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:ou:
A narrow log hull steadied by a float: the fastest thing at sea before metal. Little cargo, clumsy in tight water, and too heavy to carry or beach. The float keeps it very steady in a sea, and its raised sides seldom ship water.
- rightmouse click the halyard cleat at the mast to raise or lower the sail.
- With the sail lowered, paddle it with the paddle it carries: no oar is needed.
- Mend it with planks of its wood.
guide-goingtosea-text:
Going to Sea
The sea lets you cross. It never promises to.

The sea now has weather of its own. Wind rises and falls, storms cross the water, waves break on the shore, and every vessel can crack, flood or sink, each in its own way. A raft that is fine on a calm lake will not cross an ocean in a gale.

Before a crossing
- Read the sky and the trees: a storm shows itself before it arrives. See Wind, Storms and Currents.
- Choose a vessel that suits the trip, and check its hull. See Vessels and Their Repair.
- Take a bowl or bucket to bail with, and some material to mend the hull. See Surf, Swamping and Bailing.
- Know where you will leave the vessel. See Mooring and Anchoring.

Dangerous oceans
The Rough Seas playstyle on the new world screen makes a world with more open ocean. The Dangerous oceans world setting, on by default, decides whether the sea can harm your vessels. With it off, wind, storms and currents still come and go, but storms, lightning, surf and swamping do no harm. Rocks, rapids and weapons still crack a hull, reed still soaks and hide still seeps either way.
guide-weather-title: Rough Seas: Wind, Storms and Currents
guide-weather-text:
Wind
Wind has a direction and a strength, and it changes over hours. The stronger and the longer it blows over open water, the higher the waves, so a big lake raises a sea of its own. Trees, clouds, rain and the roll of a boat all follow it, so look around before you push off.

Storms
Storms drift across the world, born where and when real ones are.
- Squalls are small, favour warm, wet summers and pass within hours.
- Gales sweep the middle latitudes, strongest in winter, cover a great area and blow for days.
- Hurricanes form over warm tropical seas from late summer into autumn, last for days and bring the strongest wind of all.
A storm warns you first: treetops start to sway, the sky darkens and the swell rises. That is your time to make for shore.

Lightning
Warm storms bring thunder, and lightning strikes inside them. A mast draws it, and a strike can split a hull. Cold gales bring no thunder.

Currents
The oceans turn in great slow circles. The strongest current runs along an ocean's western shore, and small seas barely move. In the middle latitudes it carries warm water and the eastern side is cool; nearer the equator and nearer the poles it turns over. A vessel left alone drifts with the current, so tie it up or anchor it before you step ashore.
guide-vessels-title: Rough Seas: Vessels and Their Repair
guide-vessels-text:
Condition
Every vessel has a hull, and a knock cracks it where it lands: on the bow, a side, the quarter or the bottom. Look at a vessel to read each cracked place, from scratched through cracked and split to stove in, how many litres a minute she leaks, and her freeboard, the height of her side above the water. The hull shows each crack where it is. The condition stays with the vessel when you pick it up.

What cracks a hull
- Running into rock, shore or another vessel at speed, and the more aboard, the harder: riders, cargo and above all water in the bilge. Easing in to a landing is safe.
- Rapids, which batter the bottom of every hull except the bark canoe.
- Breaking surf, lightning, explosions and weapons.
What a hull is made of decides how much it takes: a knock that cracks a bark canoe barely scratches a sailboat. A dugout or an outrigger can be built from any tree, other mods' trees too, and the harder the wood, the tougher the hull. Wood barely wears: a wooden hull needs no upkeep.

Lost by flooding
A crack in the bottom always leaks; one in the side leaks once a load sets her low. Leaks fill her bilge until she swamps, and enough cracks outpace any bailing. Only a really severe blow breaks a hull up at once, or one that stoves in its last sound place. See Surf, Swamping and Bailing.

Rafts, reed and hide
- A raft has no hull to fill. Knocks loosen its lashings, and once they are all worked loose it comes apart into logs and rope.
- A reed boat's bundles spring back from blows, though hard knocks tear them, and it soaks up water: after about three days afloat it lies on the bottom. Ashore in the sun it dries, but rots a little each time.
- A currach's seams seep unless greased with rendered fat every few days; look at it to see when.

Mending
Hold the vessel's own material and rightmouse click its hull to mend it, one patch at a time: the patch goes on the place you look at, or on the worst crack if that place is sound. Each patch is hard work and makes you hungry, and a hull with nothing to mend says so. Flax twine binds up a raft's lashings, planks of the same wood mend a sailboat, and each boat's handbook page says what mends it. A reed boat cannot be mended. A broken vessel is gone: only floating wreckage is left.

Choosing a vessel
- Reed boat: cheap and quick, a few days afloat at a time.
- Dugout: the toughest hull on rivers and lakes, but it rolls in a sea. Burnt and hewn out of five logs beside the water.
- Coracle: turns on the spot, carried on your back.
- Bark canoe: of birch, elm or spruce bark; fast, runs rapids, fragile.
- Hide currach: carries cargo and rides over the swell.
- Outrigger canoe: fast and steady on open sea.
- Sailboat: strong and roomy, the vessel for long voyages.
guide-surf-title: Rough Seas: Surf, Swamping and Bailing
guide-surf-text:
Surf
Where shallow water meets big waves, they break. Out at sea a high swell breaks only now and then, but close to shore in rough weather every wave becomes surf. A breaking wave slams the side it hits. On a steep beach most waves plunge, and a plunging crest slams far harder: it can stave in a hide boat. Land in calm weather or in a sheltered bay.

Shipping water
When the waves run higher than a vessel's sides, water comes aboard, and cracks let it in below. Boats with a hull, from the coracle to the sailboat, hold it in their bilge: look at the vessel to see how many litres it carries and how fast it leaks, and you see the water in the boat itself. Water aboard weighs it down: it rides lower, ships more, rolls harder and gets slower. A load does the same: a loaded boat sits lower and ships water sooner, and with no freeboard left the sea comes over her side and floods her, cracked or not.

Swamping
A full bilge swamps the vessel. A light boat lies awash: it cannot be paddled or sat in, but you can hold on to it, bail it out, wait for a lull, or leave it. A sailboat heavy with ballast, a boat of wood heavier than water, or one loaded heavy goes down instead and lies on the bottom with her cargo: dive for it, or break her up there with an axe for her wreckage. Rafts and reed boats hold no water, as it washes straight through them: a raft holds its rider up even pressed under, while a reed boat soaks until it sinks.

Bailing
Hold an empty bowl, jug or bucket and keep rightmouse pressed while looking into the boat: looking at the sea, you fill the bowl from it instead. Each scoop throws water over the side. In a storm, keep bailing: an open sailboat left alone in a severe gale swamps within minutes. A bucket keeps up with one bad leak; several outpace any bailing, so mend them.
guide-mooring-text:
A vessel left alone drifts with the current, and a storm can throw it onto the shore.

Tying up
Tie a vessel to a fence post ashore with a rope, the way you tie an animal. The post holds it, but a strong enough pull snaps the rope.

Anchoring
A sailboat carries a stone anchor in its prow. rightmouse click it with an empty hand to let it go or haul it up. The anchor holds best when you let out plenty of rope, about five times the depth of the water. Its own rope reaches about 120 metres. For deeper water, stow an anchor warp at the foot of the mast with ctrl + rightmouse.
- Too little rope, and the anchor drags in a storm.
- Water deeper than the rope, and the anchor hangs and holds nothing.
- A rope that snaps takes the anchor with it.
While someone steers the vessel, the anchor does not hold it but drags along behind.

Leaving a vessel
An anchored vessel takes the waves more gently, but it still ships water. Moored close to shore with no one nearby, it may be thrown up on the beach when a storm comes. Far from shore and well anchored, it rides out the night.
